Succession

/suk-SESH-un/ — rhymes with cushion · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Succession A succession is a series of people or things following one another in order.

This succession of storms, marching across the valley over nine straight days, left basements soaked and farmers despairing over their ruined crops.

Worked Example

The kingdom's succession of rulers—first King Edward, then his son Edmund, then Edmund's daughter Eleanor—lasted nearly three centuries.

Succession emphasizes that these rulers followed one another in a definite, organized line, one naturally following the next through family authority. 'List' or 'sequence' wouldn't capture that sense of an established line of inheritance.

How Succession Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

sequence

sequence: any ordered series, without passing authority

rotation

rotation: turn-taking that cycles back around temporarily

chain

chain: linked items without an organized handover

Antonyms

interruption

interruption: a break in the continuous line

disorder

disorder: a scattered state with no order

How Strong Is It? — interruption → sequence → rotation → succession

interruption vs. succession

interruption vs. succession: An interruption is the absence of any following at all: when the relay runner dropped the baton, the chain of handoffs broke, and no succession remained.

sequence vs. succession

sequence vs. succession: The numbered steps of a recipe form a sequence — an order, nothing more — but no step hands authority to the next, so it never rises to a succession.

rotation vs. succession

rotation vs. succession: Lifeguards trading the tower chair every hour form only a rotation; each expects the post back, while a succession passes the role on for good.

Sort It Out

Now place each word on the right side of succession.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — suc- (from sub-)

Prefix — suc- (from sub-): next, after (sub- changes its spelling to suc- before a c)

Root — ced-

Root — ced-: to go

Suffix — -ion

Suffix — -ion: act or process of

Put it together

Put it together: Suc- (next, after) + ced- (to go) + -ion (act or process of) = the act or process of things going one after another — a series, or one person following another into a role. Compare its sibling successive: the same prefix and root, but swapping -ion for -ive turns the noun (the process itself) into the adjective (describing the things that follow). Once again sub- assimilates to suc- before c, giving the double c.

Use the root in a new word: intercede

Use the root in a new word: intercede: When the argument between the teammates became heated, the coach had to intercede and remind them they were on the same team.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal / neutral

Use succession when describing an orderly sequence where one thing follows another as part of an organized plan—like heirs to a throne or a chain of command. For any ordered list with no sense of passing authority or organized following, use sequence instead.
